title: Body, will and choices.
intro: How can we relate what we perceive, think, desire and do? This space connects self-control, care and Christian life through seven areas for reflection and everyday examples.
authorNote: An authorial teaching framework inspired by a reflection from Marcos Lucas Pereira. It is not an anatomical division, a scientific theory or a traditional correspondence between seven organs and seven capital sins.
distinctionTitle: Seven areas for reflection, not seven sinful body parts
distinctionText: Capital sins classify vices, not organs. A single vice can involve thought, affection, speech and action. Eyes, the nose, the stomach and sexuality are not impure parts: moral examination considers choices and conduct, not merely the presence of a sensation. This list was chosen to organize the study.
areasTitle: What arises and what I can choose
areasIntro: Some experiences are involuntary, while we can learn to guide our decisions. These are the platform’s applications, not rules for monitoring every sensation or judging someone else’s body.
areas: Thoughts and attention
An unexpected idea, memory or distraction can arise without your wanting it. Thinking something does not automatically mean agreeing with it or deciding to act.
What you choose to nurture, plan and do deserves examination. The aim is learning to respond with discernment, not preventing every unwanted thought.
Notice the thought, return attention to a manageable task and ask which action fits truth and care. Needing support is not a reason for shame.
Romans 12:2
rm/12
Looking and listening
You may notice beauty, receive an image you did not seek or hear something unpleasant. This first contact does not determine your response.
Choose the content you seek and how you treat people you see. Attraction does not authorize objectifying someone, harassment or betraying commitments.
Stop content you recognize as harmful, check information and seek selections consistent with your values without condemning whole genres or groups.
Matthew 5:27–30
mt/5
Smell, memories and surroundings
A smell may bring appetite or a memory; sensing it is not a moral failure. Sensory experiences vary between people.
Notice the context and what you need to do carefully. There is no capital sin specific to the nose or duty to eliminate all ordinary stimuli.
If surroundings are uncomfortable, adjust them or move away when possible and safe. Recognize a sensation without treating it as an order.
Mouth, words and relationships
Anger, nervousness or an urge to reply may appear before speaking. We do not need to call every emotion a sin to examine our words.
Cultivate truth, respect and responsibility in speech. Prayer can accompany learning but does not replace apologizing, correcting a lie or repairing an offence.
Before posting or replying, ask whether the message clarifies or attacks. Choose honest, respectful words; if you caused harm, seek to put it right.
James 3:1–12
tg/3
Heart, affections and intentions
Here, heart is biblical language for inner life, not an anatomical account of emotions. Affection, fear and desire do not always arise as we wish.
Examine what takes priority and the means used to pursue what you love. Loving someone gives no right to control their freedom; having resources need not become greed.
Ask who is affected and which boundary protects everyone’s dignity. Cultivate gratitude and practical help within your means.
Proverbs 4:23
pv/4
Food and bodily needs
Hunger and the need for food are not moral failures. Needs and health circumstances vary; someone’s body does not reveal their character.
Temperance can guide resource use, attention to excess and sharing. Fasting should not become punishment, competition or a substitute for health care.
Care for a meal within your circumstances, avoid waste and share when possible. See the dedicated space to study fasting and health precautions.
Isaiah 58:6–10
is/58
Sexuality, intimacy and commitments
Attraction does not oblige action or remove the body’s dignity. Reflection should respect age, privacy and personal history.

In Christian ethics, chastity concerns integrating sexuality and faithfulness according to one’s state of life, not treating the body as impure. Respect, responsibility and freedom from exploitation are essential.
Care for boundaries and commitments. Do not use faith, affection or desire to pressure another person; seek responsible guidance when questions arise.
1 Thessalonians 4:3–8
1ts/4
willTitle: Will gives direction, but does not govern everything alone
willText: Choices matter, and habits can be cultivated. Fatigue, health, circumstances, resources and support also need consideration. Promising total control of sensations, thoughts or emotions is unrealistic. In this Christian reading, self-control goes with grace, love and learning, not a contest to prove willpower.
emotionsTitle: Caring for emotions without condemning yourself
emotionsText: Feelings are not switches we choose to turn on or off. We can recognize them, make room for experience and learn more caring responses. In Catholic teaching, passions considered in themselves do not determine a person’s moral goodness or evil. This does not license aggression; it distinguishes feeling from choosing how to act.
emotionsExample: For example, anger may call for a pause and a safe conversation; sadness may call for listening, company or care. You do not need to appear cheerful to deserve respect. If distress is intense, the support space offers ways to seek human help.
steps: Notice and name: what am I feeling or wanting now?
Distinguish: did this arise without choice, or am I choosing to nurture a pattern of conduct?
Consider: who will be affected, and which action respects my values and my neighbour?
Choose one achievable step and seek support when needed, without trying to solve everything at once.
stepsNote: An educational, author-written exercise, not a psychological test, diagnosis or method of absolute control. Prayer and health care can go together.
createText: In this project, co-creation has an authorial, collaborative meaning: study carefully, produce a resource, review sources and share learning to serve others. It does not mean thought creates events, will controls everything or people create in the same way as God.
createSteps: Learn: read the source and distinguish text, interpretation and uncertainty.
Produce: write or record clearly, identifying authorship and references.
Review: welcome correction, check information and respect rights and licences.
Share: teach without humiliation and turn knowledge into care.
sourcesTitle: Where do these ideas come from?
sourcesText: The seven-area framework is an authorial proposal. Bible references support study and application. The Catechism is identified as a Catholic source; the WHO guide addresses stress management, not the classification of sin. None of these sources establishes an equivalence between seven sins and seven organs.

relationTitle: How do these areas relate to vices?
relationText: One attitude can span several areas: greed may involve comparison, cultivated desire, deceptive words and unjust choices. Anger can appear in intention, speech and action. This connection helps examine conduct; it does not mean every sensation produces sin or that a path towards aggression is inevitable.
